headline: High-risk pair: Langflow’s unsandboxed server-side execution and broad egress create dangerous default pathways for leakage, conflicts, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a content-writing source with no shared channel documented, but Agent B can ingest uploaded files and chain flow nodes server-side. If A’s outputs are copied into B’s flows, B may treat them as trusted instructions. The pairwise pathway is inferred rather than directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF Agent A outputs are pasted into Agent B flow inputs or uploaded files
IF Agent B nodes parse those inputs as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Add a fixed delimiter and instruction/data separation prompt
Disable automatic execution of pasted content in flows
Require manual review before any tool node runs
Use a quarantine workspace for imported A outputs

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B explicitly reads files, stores flow inputs/intermediate outputs, and has broad network egress; Agent A has broad network egress but no data classes touched are listed. The shared-data pathway is plausible if A content is moved into B’s filesystem or flow inputs, but the exact sensitive class is not documented, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF Agent A content includes secrets, credentials, or regulated data
IF that content is uploaded into Agent B flows or stored on B’s server filesystem
mitigations: Avoid placing sensitive A outputs into B flows
Restrict B network egress to approved endpoints
Turn off retention for uploaded files where possible
Separate workspaces and credentials between agents

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem, execute shells, spawn subprocesses, and run unsandboxed Python by default; Agent A’s profile does not show write controls, but its broad egress means it can still act externally. Because B also uses server-side shared state, overlapping writes and concurrent flow runs can corrupt shared resources. Uncertainty about A’s write surface does not reduce the risk enough to go below high.
conditions: IF Agent B instances run concurrently against the same workspace or store
IF Agent B flows write to shared files, caches, or server-side state
mitigations: Assign each flow a unique working directory
Serialize writes to shared resources
Disable or sandbox the Python code component
Mount shared storage read-only where feasible
Use per-run locks for file and state mutations

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B is a graph-based orchestrator that can chain multiple agents and tools, so A’s outputs can become B’s inputs and then drive downstream actions. Agent A is a content-writing source, making it plausible that B treats its text as authoritative. Because B can call APIs and execute shell commands, a mistaken A output can cascade into irreversible external actions.
conditions: IF Agent A output is used as an input to a downstream B node without verification
IF any B node performs API calls, shell commands, or writes based on that output
mitigations: Insert a verification step before any action node
Require citations or structured schemas from A outputs
Gate external actions behind human approval
Log and diff intermediate outputs before execution

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B stores per-flow credentials and intermediate outputs on a server-side platform with broad egress, while Agent A is an open-source content-writing artifact with no residency controls documented. The pair creates a plausible retention and data-handling mismatch if regulated data is routed through B. The evidence is indirect, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated or personal data is processed in Agent B flows
IF retention, residency, or deletion requirements apply to that data
mitigations: Do not route regulated data through B without policy review
Set explicit retention limits for flow artifacts
Document residency and subprocess hosting locations
Separate secret-bearing flows from general content workflows
